topic: A person who taught you something important
cue: Describe a person who taught you something important.
closing: and explain why this lesson was important to you.
followUps: Have you ever passed this lesson on to someone else?
Are you a good teacher yourself?
sampleAnswer: The person I'd like to talk about is my grandfather, Antonio, who was a carpenter for most of his life. I spent a lot of time with him as a child, because both of my parents worked long hours, so after school I'd usually end up in his workshop, which smelled of sawdust and varnish. I still associate that smell with him. What he taught me, on the surface, was how to make simple things out of wood, like a bird box or a small shelf. But the real lesson was about patience. I was a very impatient kid. I wanted to finish everything in five minutes, and I'd get frustrated when a joint didn't fit or a piece cracked. He never got angry. He'd just say, the wood isn't in a hurry, so why are you? Then he'd show me how to measure twice, cut slowly, and sand everything properly. I remember once I spent an entire weekend on a little stool and it was wobbly at the end. Instead of fixing it for me, he made me take it apart and find the problem myself. It was infuriating at the time, but when I finally got it right, I was incredibly proud. This lesson has turned out to be important in ways I didn't expect. At university, whenever I'm stuck on a difficult assignment or a piece of code that won't work, I hear his voice telling me to slow down. It's made me much more persistent and a lot less afraid of making mistakes. He passed away a few years ago, but I still have that stool in my bedroom, and it reminds me of him every day.

topic: A place where you like to relax
cue: Describe a place in your town or city where you like to relax.
closing: and explain why you find this place relaxing.
followUps: Do you usually go there alone or with other people?
sampleAnswer: I'm going to talk about a small public garden near my flat. It's tucked away behind an old church, so a lot of people walk past without even noticing it's there, which is part of its charm. To get in, you go through a narrow gate in a stone wall, and suddenly the noise of the traffic just fades away. It's not big, maybe the size of a couple of tennis courts, but it's full of orange trees and there's a little fountain in the middle with benches around it. I go there probably two or three times a week, usually in the late afternoon after I've finished studying. My routine is pretty simple. I grab a coffee from a café on the corner, find a bench in the shade, and either read a novel or just sit and watch what's going on. There are usually a few elderly people chatting, a couple of parents with toddlers chasing pigeons, and sometimes a student like me with a book. Occasionally, if I've got a lot on my mind, I'll leave my phone in my bag and just listen to the water. I think the reason I find it so relaxing is the contrast with the rest of my day. Most of the time I'm surrounded by screens, deadlines and crowded buses, and this garden feels like a pause button. The sound of the fountain is incredibly soothing, and in spring the smell of orange blossom is amazing. It's also free and five minutes from home, so I don't need to plan anything to go there. I honestly think it's one of the main reasons I've stayed sane during exam periods.

cue: Describe an object you own that is important to you.
bullets: how long you have had it
closing: and explain why it is important to you.
followUps: Would you ever lend this object to someone?
Do you think you will keep it for the rest of your life?
sampleAnswer: The object I'd like to describe is a rather battered old watch that belonged to my mother. It's nothing fancy, just a small silver watch with a round face and a brown leather strap that I've had to replace twice. It's not worth much money, and to be honest it loses about five minutes a week, so I have to keep adjusting it. My mum gave it to me on the day I left home to start university, which was about four years ago now. I remember we were standing at the train station, and just before I got on the train, she took it off her wrist and put it on mine. She'd worn it every day for as long as I could remember, so I was really surprised. She just said something like, now you'll always know what time it is, so no excuse for not calling me. We both laughed, but I think we were both trying not to cry. Since then I've worn it nearly every day. I took it with me when I did an exchange semester abroad, and I wore it to every single exam, partly because I need to know the time but partly as a kind of lucky charm. The reason it's so important to me is that it represents a turning point in my life. That moment at the station was when I really started being independent, and the watch reminds me that my family is behind me, even when they're far away. Whenever I'm feeling homesick or stressed, I look at it and it's oddly comforting. If I lost it, I'd be devastated, which is why I never take it to the beach.

cue: Describe a celebration or festival you enjoyed.
bullets: when and where it took place
closing: and explain why you enjoyed it so much.
followUps: Is this festival popular with young people?
sampleAnswer: I'd like to talk about a harvest festival I went to in a village in the countryside a couple of autumns ago. A friend from university, Clara, comes from this village, and she invited a few of us to stay with her family for the weekend because it was the most important event of the year there. The festival celebrates the end of the grape harvest, since the whole area is known for its wine. On the Saturday morning, the main square was decorated with vines and coloured lanterns, and there were stalls selling local cheese, bread and honey. The highlight was a kind of competition where teams had to crush grapes with their bare feet in big wooden barrels. Clara signed us up without asking, so we ended up standing in a barrel full of grapes, slipping around and laughing hysterically, while the whole village cheered. We came last, by the way, but nobody cared. In the evening, there was a long communal dinner. They put tables down the middle of the main street and everyone, from babies to great-grandparents, sat together. There was a local band playing folk music, and after dinner people started dancing. Clara's grandmother insisted on teaching me a traditional dance, and I was absolutely terrible at it. I think I enjoyed it so much because it felt so genuine. It wasn't a tourist event at all; it was a community celebrating something that really matters to them. Coming from a big city, where you don't even know your neighbours, it was moving to see a whole village come together like that. I also loved being welcomed so warmly as a complete outsider. I've been back once since then, and I'd love to make it a tradition.

cue: Describe a time when you had to make a difficult decision.
closing: and explain how you felt about the decision afterwards.
followUps: Did anyone help you make this decision?
Do you usually make decisions quickly?
sampleAnswer: One of the hardest decisions I've had to make was whether to change my degree, which happened at the end of my first year at university. I had started studying law, mainly because my father is a lawyer and everyone in my family assumed I would follow in his footsteps. I did fine in the exams, but I was honestly miserable. I found the subjects dry, and I spent most of my free time reading about psychology, which I'd always been interested in. So I had two options, really. The first was to stick with law, finish the degree, and have a fairly secure career path, possibly even joining my father's firm. The second was to start again from scratch in psychology, which meant losing a year, paying extra fees, and, of course, disappointing my dad. What made it so difficult was that both options had serious costs. I spent weeks going back and forth. I made lists of pros and cons, I talked to students in the psychology department, and I even sat in on a couple of their lectures. In the end, it was a conversation with my mother that helped me decide. She asked me to imagine myself at forty doing each job, and I realised that the thought of being a lawyer made me feel trapped. So I switched. Telling my father was one of the most awkward conversations of my life, but to his credit, he was more understanding than I expected. Looking back, I feel very relieved and proud that I made that choice. I'm far more motivated now, and my grades are better than they ever were in law. It taught me that the safe option isn't always the right one, and that it's better to make a hard decision early than to live with regret.

cue: Describe a book that had an influence on you.
closing: and explain how it influenced you.
followUps: Would you recommend this book to other people?
sampleAnswer: The book I'd like to talk about is a non-fiction book about habits, which I read during my second year of university. I won't pretend I picked it up for any noble reason. I'd been procrastinating terribly, and a friend lent it to me, half as a joke, after watching me reorganise my desk for the third time instead of studying. The basic idea of the book is that big changes in our lives come from very small habits repeated over time. The author argues that instead of setting huge goals, like I'm going to study six hours a day, you should focus on tiny, almost ridiculous steps, such as opening your book for two minutes. He also explains how our environment shapes our behaviour, so if you want to change a habit, you should make good habits easy and bad habits difficult. There are lots of examples from sport, business and everyday life, and it's written in a very accessible way. What surprised me was how practical it was. As soon as I finished it, I started experimenting. For instance, I began leaving my phone in another room while I studied, and I committed to writing just one paragraph of an essay each morning. Of course, once I'd written one paragraph, I usually kept going. Within a couple of months, my procrastination had decreased dramatically. The reason it influenced me so much is that it changed the way I think about change itself. I used to believe that people either had willpower or they didn't, and I was firmly in the second group. The book showed me that it's more about designing systems than being a heroic person. I've since used the same ideas to start running and to learn some Italian, so the effects have gone well beyond my studies.

topic: A skill that took a long time to learn
cue: Describe a skill that took you a long time to learn.
closing: and explain why it took you so long to learn.
followUps: Is this skill useful in your daily life?
Would you like to teach it to others?
sampleAnswer: The skill I want to talk about is swimming, which might sound strange, because most people learn it as small children. In my case, though, I didn't learn properly until I was about nineteen. When I was little, I had a bad experience at a crowded pool where I slipped under the water and panicked, and after that I refused to go anywhere near deep water. My parents tried to send me to lessons a couple of times, but I'd cry so much that they gave up. So I grew up as the kid who sat on the beach guarding everyone's bags. By the time I got to university, I was really embarrassed about it, so I finally signed up for adult beginner classes at the sports centre. There were about six of us, all adults, and that made it much less humiliating. The instructor was incredibly patient. For the first few weeks, we didn't even really swim. We just practised putting our faces in the water, breathing out slowly, and floating while holding onto the edge. Then gradually we moved on to kicking with a board, and eventually to front crawl. I'd say it took me almost a year before I could swim a full length without stopping and gasping for air. I think it took me so long mainly because of fear. Physically, swimming isn't that complicated, but whenever I couldn't touch the bottom, my body would tense up and I'd start to sink. Overcoming that mental block was the real challenge, and it only happened through repetition and lots of encouragement. Now I swim twice a week, and last summer I swam in the sea with my friends for the first time. It felt like a genuine victory.

topic: A journey that took longer than expected
cue: Describe a journey that took longer than you expected.
bullets: why it took longer than expected
closing: and explain how you felt during the journey.
followUps: Do you usually plan journeys carefully?
sampleAnswer: I'd like to tell you about a train journey I took a couple of winters ago, when I was travelling home to see my family for the holidays. Normally it's a four-hour trip from the city where I study, and I'd booked a direct high-speed train that was supposed to get me home in time for dinner. Well, I eventually arrived at about two in the morning. The problem started about an hour into the journey. There had been unusually heavy snowfall in the mountains, and the train suddenly stopped in the middle of nowhere. At first the announcements said it would be a short delay, maybe twenty minutes. Then it became an hour, then two. Apparently, a tree had fallen onto the line, and the heating in our carriage wasn't working properly either, so everyone was sitting there in their coats. Eventually, they told us that the line would be closed for the rest of the night, and we'd be taken back to the previous station and put on buses. So we ended up on a coach, crawling along snowy roads at about thirty kilometres an hour. At first, I was extremely frustrated, because I was really looking forward to seeing my family and I hadn't eaten anything since lunch. But then something nice happened. The passengers started chatting and sharing food. An elderly woman next to me handed out homemade biscuits, and a group of students started a card game that half the carriage joined. By the time we got on the bus, it almost felt like a party. So my feelings changed a lot during the journey, from irritation to a kind of amusement. I was exhausted when I arrived, but it's one of those trips I still tell people about, and these days I always pack snacks.

cue: Describe a building you find interesting.
closing: and explain why you find it interesting.
followUps: Would you like to live or work in this building?
Are there many buildings like this in your country?
sampleAnswer: The building I find most interesting is the central market in the city where I study. It's right in the heart of the old town, just a few streets away from the cathedral, and it was built at the beginning of the twentieth century. From the outside it's quite striking. It has a huge iron and glass structure, a bit like a railway station, with a curved roof and colourful ceramic tiles decorating the entrances, many of them showing oranges and other fruit. When the sun shines through the glass roof in the morning, the light inside is beautiful. Inside, it's basically a giant hall full of stalls, hundreds of them, selling fresh fish, meat, fruit, vegetables, spices and cheese. It's still a working market, not a museum, so local people do their daily shopping there alongside tourists who are taking photos. In recent years a few stalls have also started selling prepared food, so you can have a quick lunch of fresh seafood standing at a counter. I find it interesting for a few reasons. Architecturally, I love the combination of industrial materials, like iron and glass, with traditional decorative tiles. It's a style that was very modern at the time and shows how optimistic people were about progress. But what fascinates me even more is that it has kept its original purpose for over a hundred years. A lot of historic buildings become empty monuments, but this one is still full of life, noise and smells. Some of the stalls have been run by the same families for three or four generations, and the sellers are real characters. Whenever friends visit me, it's the first place I take them, because I think it tells you more about the city than any museum.

topic: A friend who is good at helping others
cue: Describe a friend who is good at helping other people.
closing: and explain why you think they are so helpful.
followUps: Have you ever helped this friend in return?
sampleAnswer: I'd like to describe my friend Lucas, who I met in my first week at university. We were both lost, looking for the same lecture hall, and we ended up being late together, which turned out to be a good start to a friendship. He's studying medicine now, which doesn't surprise anyone who knows him, because he's probably the most helpful person I've ever met. He helps people in all sorts of ways, big and small. On a practical level, he's the person everyone calls when they're moving flat, because he always turns up with a van he borrows from his uncle and stays until the last box is carried upstairs. He also volunteers every Sunday at a shelter for homeless people, where he helps to serve meals and sometimes just sits and chats with people who don't have anyone else to talk to. But what I appreciate most is the way he helps his friends emotionally. Last year, when I was going through a difficult time after my parents separated, he noticed before I said anything. He didn't push me to talk, but he invited me for walks almost every evening, and gradually I opened up. He's a fantastic listener; he never jumps in with advice or turns the conversation to himself. I think the reason he's so helpful is a mixture of personality and upbringing. He's naturally empathetic and genuinely curious about other people. His parents also run a small community centre in his hometown, so he grew up seeing them help others all the time, and I suppose it just became normal for him. I sometimes worry he gives too much of himself, but he says helping people gives him energy rather than taking it away.
